q: During which phase of the cardiac cycle are all four heart valves closed and ventricular volume constant while pressure rises?
why: Isovolumetric contraction starts at mitral closure (first heart sound) and ends when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure and the aortic valve opens. Isovolumetric relaxation (falling pressure) runs from aortic valve closure to mitral opening.

q: On the jugular venous waveform, which event causes the 'a' wave?
o: Atrial filling against a closed tricuspid
why: a wave: atrial contraction; c wave: tricuspid bulging in isovolumetric contraction; x descent: atrial relaxation and descent of the valve ring; v wave: atrial filling against a closed tricuspid; y descent: tricuspid opening. The a wave is absent in AF.

q: Which ion current is mainly responsible for phase 0 (rapid depolarisation) of the ventricular action potential?
why: Phase 0 in ventricular myocytes is due to fast Na⁺ influx. Phase 2 (plateau) is L-type Ca²⁺ influx balanced by K⁺ efflux; phase 3 is K⁺ efflux. In SA nodal cells, phase 0 is due to Ca²⁺ influx.

q: What produces the spontaneous depolarisation (phase 4) of sinoatrial node cells?
o: The funny current (If) and T-type calcium current
why: Phase 4 depolarisation is driven by If (HCN channels opened by hyperpolarisation), T-type Ca²⁺ current and declining K⁺ efflux. Sympathetic stimulation increases the slope; vagal stimulation reduces it. Ivabradine blocks If.

q: What is the upper limit of a normal PR interval in adults?
why: PR interval 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small squares). A PR over 0.20 s is first-degree heart block; under 0.12 s suggests pre-excitation (e.g. WPW) or a junctional rhythm. QRS is normally under 0.12 s.

q: Which ECG change is typical of hyperkalaemia?
why: Hyperkalaemia progresses from peaked T waves to flattened P waves, prolonged PR, broad QRS, sine wave and VF/asystole. Hypokalaemia causes flattened T waves, ST depression and U waves. J (Osborn) waves suggest hypothermia.

q: In chronic mitral regurgitation, what is the main haemodynamic goal during anaesthesia?
o: Slow heart rate and high afterload
why: In MR, a faster heart rate reduces regurgitant volume and LV size; reducing afterload favours forward flow. Bradycardia and raised SVR increase the regurgitant fraction. Keep preload adequate.

q: In acute severe mitral regurgitation (e.g. papillary muscle rupture), why do patients develop sudden pulmonary oedema?
o: A small, stiff left atrium sees a sudden volume load
The left atrium is large and compliant
why: In acute MR, the normal-sized, non-compliant left atrium sees a sudden volume load, so LA pressure and pulmonary venous pressure rise sharply. In chronic MR, the LA dilates and compliance increases, protecting the lungs.

q: What defines severe aortic stenosis by echocardiography?
why: Severe AS: AVA under 1.0 cm² (indexed under 0.6 cm²/m²), mean gradient over 40 mmHg, peak velocity over 4 m/s. Low-flow, low-gradient AS occurs with reduced LV function or small, stiff ventricles.

q: Which haemodynamic goal is most important when anaesthetising a patient with severe aortic stenosis?
o: Sinus rhythm, normal-to-slow rate, maintained SVR
why: The hypertrophied LV depends on atrial contraction and adequate diastolic time for coronary perfusion. Hypotension reduces coronary perfusion, causing ischaemia and a downward spiral. Treat hypotension promptly with a vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine or metaraminol.

q: Where are the arterial baroreceptors that respond to changes in blood pressure located?
why: High-pressure baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (afferents via the glossopharyngeal nerve) and the aortic arch (vagus). Carotid and aortic bodies are chemoreceptors.

q: In ATLS class III haemorrhagic shock in an adult, what is the approximate blood loss?
why: Class III (30–40%) causes tachycardia over 120, hypotension, tachypnoea, oliguria and confusion. Class II (15–30%) has a narrowed pulse pressure but normal systolic pressure. Beta-blockers, the elderly and athletes may mask tachycardia.

q: In a normal person, what happens to heart rate during phase II (sustained strain) of the Valsalva manoeuvre?
o: It rises only in phase IV
why: Phase I: BP rises transiently from increased intrathoracic pressure. Phase II: venous return falls, BP falls, and reflex tachycardia restores BP. Phase III: BP dips on release. Phase IV: overshoot of BP with reflex bradycardia.

q: What is the 'square wave' response to the Valsalva manoeuvre seen in?
why: In heart failure with high filling pressures, BP rises in phase I and stays high throughout strain without reflex change (square wave). In autonomic neuropathy, BP falls in phase II without tachycardia and there is no phase IV overshoot.

q: In the fetal circulation, oxygenated blood from the placenta bypasses the liver via which structure?
why: Oxygenated blood travels in the umbilical vein; about half bypasses the liver via the ductus venosus to the IVC. It then crosses the foramen ovale to the left atrium. The ductus arteriosus shunts pulmonary artery blood to the aorta.

q: What is the main stimulus for closure of the ductus arteriosus after birth?
o: Rise in PaO2 and fall in circulating prostaglandin E2
why: The ductus constricts functionally within about 12–24 h in response to higher PaO2 and reduced PGE2 (placenta removed, lung metabolism increases). PGE1 infusion keeps it open in duct-dependent lesions; indomethacin or ibuprofen can close it.

q: A large 'cannon a wave' in the JVP indicates what?
why: Cannon a waves occur when the atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve due to AV dissociation (complete heart block, VT, junctional rhythm). Large v waves suggest tricuspid regurgitation.

q: What is Kussmaul's sign?
o: A rise in JVP on inspiration
A fall in systolic BP over 10 mmHg on inspiration
why: Kussmaul's sign (paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration) occurs in constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy and severe right heart failure. A fall in systolic BP of over 10 mmHg on inspiration is pulsus paradoxus (e.g. tamponade).

q: According to the Starling equation, which force tends to move fluid out of the capillary?
why: Net filtration = Kf[(Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)]. Capillary hydrostatic pressure and interstitial oncotic pressure favour filtration; plasma oncotic pressure and interstitial hydrostatic pressure oppose it. The glycocalyx refines this model.

q: Approximately how much fluid does the lymphatic system return to the circulation each day?
why: About 2–4 L/day of filtered fluid and protein returns via lymph, mainly through the thoracic duct into the left subclavian–internal jugular junction. Lymphatic failure causes oedema.

q: What triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in cardiac muscle?
o: Direct mechanical coupling to DHP receptors as in skeletal muscle
Calcium-induced calcium release via ryanodine receptors after L-type channel influx
why: In cardiac muscle, Ca²⁺ entering via L-type channels triggers Ca²⁺ release through ryanodine (RyR2) receptors. In skeletal muscle, DHP receptors are mechanically linked to RyR1 and extracellular calcium is not required.

q: What does the Frank–Starling law describe?
o: Heart rate rises with venous return
Afterload is proportional to wall thickness
Coronary flow depends on diastolic pressure
Stroke volume rises with preload, up to a point
why: Greater stretch improves actin–myosin overlap and calcium sensitivity, increasing contraction force. Beyond optimal length, performance falls. The Bowditch (staircase) effect describes increased force with heart rate.

sb: Autonomic & Hormonal Regulation of Cardiac Function
q: Stimulation of which receptor increases heart rate and contractility?
why: Beta-1 receptors (Gs, cAMP rise) increase rate, contractility, conduction and relaxation. M2 muscarinic receptors (Gi) slow the heart. Alpha-1 receptors mediate vasoconstriction.

sb: Autonomic & Hormonal Regulation of Cardiac Function
q: What is the Bainbridge reflex?
o: Bradycardia from pressure on the globe
Tachycardia from increased right atrial filling
why: Stretch receptors in the right atrium and great veins increase heart rate via vagal afferents when venous return increases. The baroreceptor reflex usually dominates in humans.

q: What is the main mediator of coronary vasodilatation in response to increased myocardial metabolism?
why: Coronary blood flow is mainly regulated by local metabolic factors (adenosine, NO, K⁺, CO2, hypoxia). Myocardial oxygen extraction is already about 70% at rest, so increased demand must be met by increased flow.

q: What is the normal coronary blood flow at rest in an adult?
why: Coronary blood flow is about 250 mL/min (80 mL/100 g/min), about 5% of cardiac output. Coronary sinus blood has very low oxygen saturation (about 30%), reflecting high extraction.

q: In West zone 1 of the lung, which pressure relationship applies?
why: Zone 1: alveolar pressure exceeds arterial pressure, so there is no flow (alveolar dead space), which can occur with hypovolaemia or high PEEP. Zone 2: Pa > PA > Pv (flow depends on Pa − PA). Zone 3: Pa > Pv > PA (flow depends on Pa − Pv).

q: What is hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction mainly triggered by?
why: HPV is triggered mainly by low alveolar PO2 (and to a lesser extent mixed venous PO2), redirecting blood to better-ventilated areas. It is inhibited by volatile agents at high concentrations, vasodilators and alkalosis. It is important during one-lung ventilation.

q: In cardiopulmonary exercise testing, what does the anaerobic threshold represent?
o: The VO2 above which lactate adds extra CO2
The rate of maximal lactate clearance
The point where ventilation stops rising
why: Above the anaerobic threshold, lactate is buffered by bicarbonate, producing extra CO2 and a disproportionate rise in VCO2 and ventilation (V-slope method). An AT below about 10–11 mL/kg/min is associated with higher perioperative risk.

q: During maximal exercise in a healthy adult, which factor limits peak oxygen consumption most?
why: In healthy individuals, peak VO2 is usually limited by cardiac output (oxygen delivery). Ventilatory reserve remains at peak exercise. In lung disease, ventilation may limit exercise.

q: Which lung volume cannot be measured by simple spirometry?
why: Residual volume (and therefore FRC and TLC) cannot be measured by spirometry because it cannot be exhaled. It is measured by helium dilution, nitrogen washout or body plethysmography.

q: What is the approximate functional residual capacity of a 70 kg adult in the upright position?
why: FRC is about 30 mL/kg (about 2.5 L upright). It falls by about 0.5–1 L supine and further with anaesthesia (about 20%), obesity and pregnancy. Closing capacity rises with age and smoking.

sb: Lung Compliance, Laplace's Law & Work of Breathing
q: What is the approximate normal total compliance of the respiratory system in an adult?
why: Lung compliance and chest wall compliance are each about 200 mL/cmH2O; combined in series (1/Ct = 1/Cl + 1/Ccw), total compliance is about 100 mL/cmH2O. Static compliance is measured at zero flow.

sb: Lung Compliance, Laplace's Law & Work of Breathing
q: Which factor increases lung compliance?
why: Emphysema destroys elastic tissue, increasing compliance (but causing airway collapse and gas trapping). Fibrosis, oedema, surfactant deficiency and atelectasis reduce compliance.

sb: Hypoxia, Oxygen Delivery & the Oxyhaemoglobin Dissociation Curve
q: What is the P50 of normal adult haemoglobin?
why: P50 (PO2 at 50% saturation) is about 3.5 kPa (26.6 mmHg). Fetal haemoglobin has a lower P50 (about 2.5 kPa). A raised P50 indicates a right shift (reduced affinity).

sb: Hypoxia, Oxygen Delivery & the Oxyhaemoglobin Dissociation Curve
q: Which change shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right?
why: A right shift (reduced affinity, easier unloading to tissues) is caused by increased CO2, H⁺, temperature and 2,3-DPG. Alkalosis, hypothermia, CO, methaemoglobin and HbF shift it left.

q: How many ATP molecules are produced (net) from one glucose molecule by anaerobic glycolysis?
why: Anaerobic glycolysis yields 2 net ATP and lactate. Complete aerobic oxidation (glycolysis, Krebs cycle, oxidative phosphorylation) yields about 30–32 ATP (older textbooks quote 36–38).

q: Where does the Krebs (citric acid) cycle take place?
why: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix; the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane.

sb: Compensatory Mechanisms to Hypoxia & CO2 Homeostasis
q: Which response occurs early in acute ascent to high altitude?
why: Hypoxaemia stimulates the carotid bodies, causing hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. Over days, renal bicarbonate excretion compensates, 2,3-DPG rises, and erythropoietin increases red cell mass over weeks. HPV raises pulmonary pressure.

sb: Compensatory Mechanisms to Hypoxia & CO2 Homeostasis
q: In chronic CO2 retention (e.g. COPD), what is mainly responsible for the persisting ventilatory drive?
why: In chronic hypercapnia, CSF bicarbonate rises, normalising CSF pH and blunting the central response. Peripheral hypoxic drive contributes more. Oxygen-induced hypercapnia is mainly due to V/Q worsening and the Haldane effect rather than loss of hypoxic drive alone.

q: In hyperbaric oxygen at 3 atmospheres absolute breathing 100% oxygen, approximately how much oxygen is dissolved in plasma?
why: Dissolved oxygen = 0.0225 mL/dL/kPa × PaO2. At 3 ATA, PaO2 is about 260–280 kPa, giving about 6 mL/dL, enough to meet resting tissue needs without haemoglobin.

q: What happens to the delivered concentration from a conventional variable bypass vaporiser at altitude (low barometric pressure)?
o: Partial pressure stays about the same
why: SVP depends only on temperature, so the vaporiser delivers about the same partial pressure, which is what determines anaesthetic effect. The volume percentage rises because barometric pressure is lower. Desflurane (Tec 6) delivers a fixed volume percentage, so its partial pressure falls at altitude.

q: Approximately how much oxygen does 1 g of fully saturated haemoglobin carry?
why: Hüfner's constant is 1.34–1.39 mL O2/g Hb. Oxygen content = (1.34 × Hb × SaO2) + (0.0225 × PaO2 in kPa). With Hb 150 g/L and saturation 98%, content is about 200 mL/L.

q: What is the structure of adult haemoglobin A?
o: Two alpha and two beta chains
Two alpha and two gamma chains
Two beta and two gamma chains
Two alpha and two delta chains
why: HbA is α2β2 (about 97%); HbA2 is α2δ2 (about 2.5%); HbF is α2γ2. Each subunit has a haem group with Fe²⁺ binding one oxygen molecule, giving cooperative binding (sigmoid curve).

q: In what form is most CO2 carried in arterial blood?
why: About 90% of CO2 in arterial blood is carried as bicarbonate, about 5% as carbamino compounds and about 5% dissolved. Carbamino compounds contribute disproportionately to the arteriovenous difference.

q: What does the Haldane effect describe?
o: Chloride enters red cells as bicarbonate leaves
CO2 shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right
why: Deoxygenated haemoglobin is a better buffer and forms carbamino compounds more readily, increasing CO2 carriage in venous blood. The Bohr effect is CO2/H⁺ reducing oxygen affinity. The chloride shift describes Cl⁻ entering red cells.

q: On a flow–volume loop, a fixed upper airway obstruction (e.g. tracheal stenosis) produces what pattern?
why: Fixed obstruction limits both phases. Variable extrathoracic obstruction (e.g. vocal cord palsy) flattens inspiration; variable intrathoracic obstruction (e.g. tumour of the lower trachea) flattens expiration. Obstructive lung disease scoops the expiratory limb.

q: What is the FEV1/FVC ratio in restrictive lung disease?
why: In restrictive disease both FEV1 and FVC fall, so the ratio is normal or high. In obstructive disease FEV1 falls more than FVC, so the ratio is below 0.7.

q: Which result is typical of emphysema on pulmonary function testing?
o: Increased TLC and RV, and reduced TLCO
why: Emphysema causes airflow obstruction, hyperinflation (raised TLC, RV and RV/TLC) and reduced gas transfer due to alveolar destruction. Asthma usually has normal or raised TLCO. Fibrosis reduces TLC and TLCO.

q: In pulmonary fibrosis, how does the transfer coefficient (KCO) typically behave?
why: In interstitial fibrosis, TLCO and usually KCO are reduced. In extrapulmonary restriction (e.g. chest wall disease, neuromuscular weakness), KCO is normal or raised because the alveolar–capillary unit is normal.

sb: Effect of IPPV on the Lungs
q: How does positive pressure ventilation affect venous return?
o: It increases venous return by raising intrathoracic pressure
It only affects pulmonary venous return
It reduces venous return by raising intrathoracic and right atrial pressure
why: Raised intrathoracic pressure increases RA pressure, reducing the gradient for venous return, so cardiac output can fall, especially in hypovolaemia. It also reduces LV afterload, which can benefit a failing LV.

sb: Effect of IPPV on the Lungs
q: Which ventilation strategy reduces ventilator-induced lung injury in ARDS?
o: 6 mL/kg PBW with plateau under 30 cmH2O
why: ARDSNet showed reduced mortality with 6 mL/kg PBW and plateau under 30 cmH2O. Mechanisms of injury include volutrauma, barotrauma, atelectrauma and biotrauma. Driving pressure under about 15 cmH2O is associated with better outcomes.

q: Where is the main respiratory rhythm generator located?
o: Pneumotaxic centre in the upper pons
why: The pre-Bötzinger complex in the ventrolateral medulla generates respiratory rhythm. Dorsal and ventral respiratory groups shape the output; the pontine respiratory group (pneumotaxic centre) modulates timing; the cortex allows voluntary control.

q: What is the approximate slope of the ventilatory response to CO2 in an awake adult?
why: Minute ventilation rises by roughly 2–3 L/min per mmHg (15–20 L/min per kPa) rise in PaCO2. Opioids, volatile agents, sleep and chronic hypercapnia shift the curve right and flatten it.

q: What do the central chemoreceptors respond to?
why: Central chemoreceptors on the ventral medulla respond to CSF pH. CO2 crosses the blood–brain barrier readily and forms H⁺ in poorly buffered CSF. They provide about 80% of the response to CO2 and do not respond to hypoxia.

q: Which statement about the peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) is correct?
o: They lie on the ventral medulla
They respond quickly to low PaO2, CO2 and H⁺
They respond to O2 content, not PaO2
why: Carotid bodies (glossopharyngeal afferents) have a very high blood flow and respond to PaO2 rather than content (so anaemia and CO poisoning do not stimulate them much). They also respond to H⁺ and CO2. Low-dose volatile agents blunt the hypoxic response.

q: Which substance is inactivated during a single passage through the pulmonary circulation?
why: Pulmonary endothelium inactivates bradykinin, serotonin, noradrenaline (partly) and prostaglandins E and F. Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II by ACE. Adrenaline, vasopressin, angiotensin II and histamine pass largely unchanged.

q: Which is a non-respiratory function of the lung?
o: Filtering emboli and converting angiotensin I
why: Non-respiratory functions include filtration, metabolism (ACE, inactivation of mediators), reservoir of blood, immune defence, surfactant synthesis, heat and water loss, and drug uptake (e.g. first-pass uptake of fentanyl, lidocaine).

q: According to the Berlin definition, which PaO2/FiO2 ratio defines moderate ARDS?
why: Berlin (with PEEP at least 5 cmH2O): mild 200–300 mmHg (26.7–40 kPa), moderate 100–200 mmHg (13.3–26.7 kPa), severe 100 mmHg or less (13.3 kPa or less). Onset within 1 week, bilateral opacities, not fully explained by cardiac failure.

q: What is the main pathological feature of the exudative phase of ARDS?
o: Diffuse alveolar damage and hyaline membranes
why: The exudative phase (days 1–7) shows diffuse alveolar damage, increased permeability, neutrophil infiltration and hyaline membranes. A proliferative phase follows, then fibrosis in some patients.

q: What is the main hormone responsible for gluconeogenesis during fasting?
why: Glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Cortisol, adrenaline and growth hormone also oppose insulin. Liver glycogen stores last about 24 h of fasting.

q: During prolonged starvation, which fuel increasingly supplies the brain?
why: After a few days, ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate) from hepatic fatty acid oxidation provide much of the brain's energy, reducing protein breakdown for gluconeogenesis. Fatty acids do not cross the blood–brain barrier well.

q: Where in the nephron is most filtered sodium reabsorbed?
o: Descending limb of loop of Henle
Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
why: About 65% of filtered sodium and water are reabsorbed in the PCT, 25% in the thick ascending limb (NKCC2, target of loop diuretics), 5% in the DCT (NCC, thiazides) and 2–3% in the collecting duct (ENaC, aldosterone).

q: What is the renal threshold for glucose, above which glycosuria occurs?
why: Glucose is reabsorbed by SGLT2 (and SGLT1) in the PCT. Above a plasma level of about 10 mmol/L, transport saturates and glucose appears in the urine. SGLT2 inhibitors lower this threshold deliberately.

q: Which change reduces glomerular filtration rate?
why: Afferent constriction (e.g. NSAIDs blocking vasodilator prostaglandins, sympathetic stimulation) lowers glomerular pressure and GFR. Efferent constriction (angiotensin II) maintains GFR; ACE inhibitors reduce it in renal artery stenosis.

q: Antidiuretic hormone increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct by which mechanism?
why: ADH binds V2 receptors (Gs, cAMP), causing aquaporin-2 vesicles to fuse with the apical membrane of collecting duct cells. Aquaporin-1 in the PCT and descending limb is constitutive. V1 receptors mediate vasoconstriction.

q: Which segment of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water but actively transports NaCl out, creating the medullary gradient?
why: The thick ascending limb pumps NaCl out via NKCC2 but is impermeable to water, diluting tubular fluid and concentrating the interstitium. The descending limb is water-permeable, so fluid concentrates as it descends (countercurrent multiplication).

q: What is the approximate maximum osmolality of urine that the human kidney can produce?
why: The medullary gradient reaches about 1200 mOsm/kg at the papilla, so maximally concentrated urine is about 1200 mOsm/kg. Minimum urine osmolality is about 50 mOsm/kg. Urea recycling contributes about half of the gradient.

sb: Liver Anatomy, Blood Supply & Metabolic Functions
q: What proportion of hepatic blood flow comes from the hepatic artery?
why: The hepatic artery provides about 25% of flow (but about 50% of the oxygen); the portal vein provides about 75% of flow. Total hepatic blood flow is about 1.5 L/min (25% of cardiac output). The hepatic arterial buffer response compensates for falls in portal flow.

sb: Liver Anatomy, Blood Supply & Metabolic Functions
q: Which zone of the liver acinus is most vulnerable to hypoxic injury and paracetamol toxicity?
why: Zone 3, nearest the central vein, receives the least oxygenated blood and has the highest cytochrome P450 activity, generating toxic NAPQI from paracetamol. Zone 1 is affected first by direct toxins carried in portal blood.

q: In what form is bilirubin transported in plasma before reaching the liver?
why: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and albumin-bound. The liver conjugates it with glucuronic acid (UGT1A1) to water-soluble conjugated bilirubin, excreted in bile. Gut bacteria convert it to urobilinogen.

q: A patient has jaundice, dark urine and pale stools. Which type of jaundice is most likely?
why: Obstruction causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; water-soluble conjugated bilirubin enters urine (dark), and no bilirubin reaches the gut (pale stools). Haemolytic jaundice causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without bilirubinuria.

q: What is the main route of lactate clearance in the body?
why: The liver clears about 60% of lactate (gluconeogenesis via the Cori cycle), with the kidneys and heart also oxidising it. Liver failure reduces clearance and can cause hyperlactataemia.

q: How does the liver mainly detoxify ammonia?
o: Conversion to urea in the urea cycle
why: The urea cycle in periportal hepatocytes converts ammonia to urea, excreted by the kidneys. Glutamine synthesis in perivenous hepatocytes, muscle and brain provides a second route. Hyperammonaemia contributes to hepatic encephalopathy.

q: Which cells secrete hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
why: Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete HCl via the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase (target of PPIs) and intrinsic factor. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen; G cells secrete gastrin; ECL cells secrete histamine.

q: What is the normal gastric emptying half-time for clear fluids?
why: Clear fluids empty exponentially with a half-time of about 10–20 min, supporting fasting guidance allowing clear fluids up to 2 hours before surgery (1 hour in children under recent guidance). Solids empty more slowly.

q: Where is the chemoreceptor trigger zone located?
why: The CTZ lies in the area postrema outside the blood–brain barrier, detecting circulating emetogens. It contains dopamine D2, 5-HT3, opioid and NK1 receptors and projects to the vomiting centre in the medulla.

q: Which antiemetic acts as an NK1 receptor antagonist?
why: Aprepitant blocks substance P at NK1 receptors. Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3; cyclizine blocks H1 and muscarinic receptors; droperidol blocks D2; dexamethasone's mechanism is uncertain.

sb: CNS Physiology: Motor End Plate & Nerve Fibres
q: Which nerve fibre type conducts fastest?
why: A-alpha fibres (motor, proprioception) are the largest myelinated fibres (12–20 µm) and conduct at 70–120 m/s. A-delta carries fast pain (5–30 m/s); C fibres are unmyelinated and slowest (0.5–2 m/s).

sb: CNS Physiology: Motor End Plate & Nerve Fibres
q: At the neuromuscular junction, what triggers acetylcholine release from the nerve terminal?
why: Depolarisation opens P/Q-type calcium channels; Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion via SNARE proteins. Magnesium and aminoglycosides reduce release; Lambert–Eaton syndrome involves antibodies to these channels; botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins.

sb: The Reflex Arc & Autonomic Nervous System
q: Which neurotransmitter is released by preganglionic sympathetic neurons at the ganglion?
why: All preganglionic autonomic fibres release acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors. Most sympathetic postganglionic fibres release noradrenaline; those to sweat glands release acetylcholine. The adrenal medulla acts as a modified ganglion.

sb: The Reflex Arc & Autonomic Nervous System
q: The knee jerk reflex is an example of which reflex type?
why: Stretch of muscle spindles activates Ia afferents synapsing directly on alpha motor neurons (L3–L4). Golgi tendon organs mediate inhibitory (Ib) reflexes. Withdrawal reflexes are polysynaptic.

q: How does smooth muscle contraction differ from skeletal muscle contraction?
o: Calcium binds troponin C to move tropomyosin
Calcium–calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase
Contraction is always under voluntary control
Sarcomeres are arranged in regular bands
why: In smooth muscle, Ca²⁺ binds calmodulin, activating MLCK, which phosphorylates myosin light chains. Smooth muscle lacks troponin and sarcomeres. The 'latch' state maintains tone with low ATP use.

q: Which glial cell forms myelin in the peripheral nervous system?
why: Schwann cells myelinate one segment of one peripheral axon. Oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple CNS axons. Myelin increases conduction velocity by saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.

sb: The Brain: Anatomy, Blood Flow & Intracranial Pressure
q: Between which mean arterial pressures is cerebral blood flow autoregulated in normal adults (classical range)?
why: The classical range is a MAP of about 50–150 mmHg (some recent data suggest a narrower plateau, about 70–150). Chronic hypertension shifts the curve to the right. Autoregulation is impaired by volatile agents at high doses, TBI and hypercapnia.

sb: The Brain: Anatomy, Blood Flow & Intracranial Pressure
q: How does cerebral blood flow change with PaCO2 in the physiological range?
why: CBF changes by about 1–2 mL/100 g/min per mmHg (about 15–30% per kPa) between PaCO2 of about 3–10 kPa. Hyperventilation reduces CBF and ICP transiently but risks ischaemia, so it is reserved for impending herniation.

q: Which pathway carries pain and temperature sensation to the thalamus?
why: First-order neurons synapse in the dorsal horn; second-order fibres cross within one or two segments and ascend in the contralateral spinothalamic tract to the thalamus. Dorsal columns carry fine touch, vibration and proprioception, crossing in the medulla.

q: What does the gate control theory of pain propose?
o: Descending pathways can only increase pain
Pain is processed only in the cortex
Pain is transmitted only by C fibres
A-beta input closes a dorsal horn gate on pain
Opioids act only on peripheral nerves
why: Melzack and Wall proposed that A-beta activity closes the 'gate' in lamina II, which explains relief from rubbing and TENS. Descending inhibition from the periaqueductal grey and rostral ventromedial medulla (serotonin, noradrenaline, opioids) also modulates pain.

q: Which mechanism contributes to central sensitisation (wind-up)?
o: Reduced glutamate release from C fibres
NMDA receptor activation in the dorsal horn
why: Repeated C-fibre stimulation removes the Mg²⁺ block of NMDA receptors, increasing dorsal horn excitability, causing hyperalgesia and allodynia. Ketamine (an NMDA antagonist) can reduce this.

q: Which feature is characteristic of neuropathic pain?
o: Colicky pain from a hollow viscus
Pain that resolves with the inflammation
why: Neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease of the somatosensory system and is described as burning, shooting or electric, often with allodynia and sensory loss. First-line drugs include amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin and pregabalin.

q: What is the molecular abnormality in sickle cell disease?
o: Deletion of all four alpha genes
Glu6Val point mutation in beta globin
why: HbS results from a point mutation (Glu6Val) on the beta chain. Deoxygenated HbS polymerises, deforming red cells. Precipitants include hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration, cold and infection.

q: What preoperative transfusion strategy is recommended for patients with HbSS having medium-risk surgery?
o: Top-up transfusion to Hb about 100 g/L
Transfuse only if Hb under 50 g/L
why: The TAPS trial supported preoperative top-up transfusion to about 100 g/L for HbSS patients having low- or medium-risk surgery. Exchange transfusion may be used for high-risk surgery or if baseline Hb is high. Avoid hypoxia, hypothermia, dehydration and acidosis.

q: Which antibodies cause a severe acute haemolytic transfusion reaction from ABO incompatibility?
why: Naturally occurring IgM anti-A and anti-B fix complement, causing intravascular haemolysis, hypotension, fever, DIC and renal failure. The commonest cause is wrong-patient identification. Stop the transfusion and give supportive care.

q: Group O RhD-negative red cells are used in emergencies because they lack which antigens?
o: A and B antigens, and RhD
why: Group O red cells lack A and B antigens, so they are not haemolysed by recipient anti-A or anti-B. RhD-negative units are given to females of childbearing potential to avoid sensitisation. Group AB plasma is the universal plasma donor.

q: Which test is used to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy?
why: The APTT measures the intrinsic and common pathways and is prolonged by UFH (anti-Xa levels are an alternative). The PT/INR monitors warfarin. LMWH, if monitored, uses anti-Xa levels.

q: Which clotting factors are vitamin K dependent?
o: II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S)
why: Vitamin K enables gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S. Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 6 h), so the INR rises first with warfarin. Prothrombin complex concentrate replaces II, VII, IX and X.

q: Which immunoglobulin crosses the placenta?
why: IgG crosses the placenta via neonatal Fc receptors, giving passive immunity and also explaining haemolytic disease of the newborn (anti-D). IgM is the first antibody in a primary response; IgA protects mucosa; IgE mediates type I hypersensitivity.

q: Which cells are the main effectors of cell-mediated immunity against virally infected cells?
why: CD8 T cells recognise antigen on MHC class I and kill infected cells. CD4 helper T cells recognise MHC class II and coordinate responses. Natural killer cells kill cells lacking MHC I. B cells become plasma cells producing antibody.

q: In anaphylaxis, which mediator is measured to support the diagnosis?
why: Mast cell tryptase peaks about 1–2 h after the reaction; NAP6 recommends samples at the reaction, 1–2 h and 24 h (or at follow-up). Histamine has a very short half-life. Referral to an allergy clinic is required.

q: What is the recommended reversal for life-threatening bleeding in a patient taking warfarin?
o: Four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K
why: Four-factor PCC (25–50 units/kg, dose by INR) plus 5–10 mg IV vitamin K reverses warfarin rapidly. Protamine reverses heparin; idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors where available.

q: Which hormone level typically falls during the surgical stress response?
why: The stress response increases catabolic hormones (cortisol, ACTH, catecholamines, glucagon, GH, ADH), while insulin secretion falls relatively and insulin resistance develops, causing hyperglycaemia. Neuraxial blocks can attenuate the response to lower-body surgery.

q: Which metabolic effect is part of the stress response to major surgery?
o: Catabolism, hyperglycaemia, salt and water retention
why: Catabolism causes muscle breakdown and negative nitrogen balance; hyperglycaemia arises from gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance; ADH and aldosterone cause salt and water retention and potassium loss. Cytokines (IL-6) drive the acute phase response.

q: Which hormone is the main regulator of plasma ionised calcium?
why: PTH raises calcium by increasing bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption and renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D (increasing gut absorption). It also increases phosphate excretion. Calcitonin has a minor role in humans.

q: Where does most circulating T3 come from?
why: The thyroid secretes mainly T4; about 80% of T3 comes from peripheral deiodination. T3 is more potent. In critical illness, conversion falls and reverse T3 rises (sick euthyroid syndrome).

q: Which hormone is produced by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex?
why: 'GFR': zona glomerulosa makes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), fasciculata makes glucocorticoids (cortisol) and reticularis makes androgens. The medulla makes catecholamines, mainly adrenaline (via PNMT, induced by cortisol).

q: Which enzyme converts noradrenaline to adrenaline in the adrenal medulla?
why: Synthesis: tyrosine → L-DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate limiting) → dopamine (DOPA decarboxylase) → noradrenaline (dopamine beta-hydroxylase) → adrenaline (PNMT). MAO and COMT break down catecholamines.

q: Which molecule mediates platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen under high shear?
why: vWF bridges collagen and platelet GPIb. Platelets are then activated, releasing ADP and TXA2, and GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen to aggregate platelets. Aspirin blocks TXA2 synthesis; clopidogrel blocks P2Y12.

q: Which statement about the cell-based model of coagulation is correct?
o: Platelets play no role in thrombin generation
Factor XII is essential for haemostasis in vivo
Initiation on TF-bearing cells, propagation on platelets
why: Initiation: TF–VIIa generates a little thrombin on TF-bearing cells. Amplification: thrombin activates platelets and factors V, VIII and XI. Propagation: tenase and prothrombinase on platelets produce a thrombin burst. Factor XII deficiency does not cause bleeding.
